extracted.intended_audience: students and general readers learning introductory astronomy (and related natural philosophy)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and explanations for studying the planets (particularly Mercury and Venus), their motions, visibility, phases, transits, and related observational and pedagogical advice. Also includes explanatory criteria for tidal behaviour earlier in the text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pedagogical order for learning astronomy
rubrics_metrics.description: Begin with earth, sun, and moon and the doctrine of the sphere; acquire familiar terms and definitions before advancing to planetary motions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author recommends a lucid arrangement: bring facts and doctrines where the learner is prepared to receive them; frequently review earlier parts until they become familiar; do not avoid the necessity of thinking. Reiterate earlier parts before advancing to more intricate subjects to gain clear perception of subsequent topics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'planet' (wanderer)
rubrics_metrics.description: A planet is a 'wanderer' (Greek planêtês) — a body that shifts its positions in the heavens as opposed to fixed stars which maintain the same places relative to each other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as the basic classificatory definition; underlies expectations of planetary motion relative to stars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary vs secondary planets classification
rubrics_metrics.description: Primary planets: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and (as of the author's time) Ceres, Pallas, Juno, Vesta. Secondary planets: satellites that revolve around primary planets (e.g., Moon, Jupiter's four, Saturn's seven, Uranus's six).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Totals given: eleven primary and eighteen secondary planets, making twenty-nine altogether (period historical to the text). This is the classificatory criterion for counting and distinguishing bodies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Planets remain near the ecliptic — observational expectation
rubrics_metrics.description: You should not look for a planet very far north or very far south because planets are always near the ecliptic; Mercury never more than ~7°, Venus ~47° (and some new planets have larger inclinations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observers should search along the ecliptic; the maximum deviations govern visibility and search strategy (note Pallas deviates up to 34.5°).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inferior vs superior planets (orbit-based distinction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Inferior planets have orbits nearer the sun than the earth (Mercury and Venus); superior planets have orbits farther from the sun than the earth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This distinction explains many observational phenomena (appearance near sun, phases, conjunction behaviour). It is a primary organizing criterion for planetary behaviour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visibility of inferior planets — observe at greatest elongations
rubrics_metrics.description: Mercury and Venus are visible only when near their greatest elongations from the sun; consult almanac for times of greatest elongation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mercury seldom visible in high latitudes; both appear in west after sunset or east before sunrise. Mercury visible for several evenings if watched at its greatest elongation; otherwise lost in sunlight. Diagrams (Fig. 50) explain geometry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conjunction types and definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: A planet is in conjunction with the sun when seen in the same part of the heavens; inferior conjunction when on the same side of the sun as the earth; superior conjunction when on the side of the sun most distant from the earth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These definitions are used to explain synodical behaviour, phases, and apparent motion (direct/retrograde) of inferior planets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sidereal vs synodical revolution (period definitions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sidereal revolution: time for one circuit relative to the stars. Synodical revolution: time between successive conjunctions with the earth. Synodical > sidereal because the earth moves while the planet orbits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explained with analogy to clock hands and illustrated (Mercury sidereal ~88 days, synodical ~116 days; Venus synodical ~584 days). Useful for predicting appearances and conjunction intervals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct vs retrograde motion of inferior planets
rubrics_metrics.description: Motion is 'direct' when in order of signs from west to east; 'retrograde' when contrary (east to west). An inferior planet moves direct through superior conjunction and retrograde through inferior conjunction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author explains why apparent retrograde occurs, how earth's motion modifies apparent motion, and why stationary points occur; diagrams and geometric reasoning provided (Fig. 51).

rubrics_metrics.name: Stationary points occur near greatest elongations (with degrees)
rubrics_metrics.description: When passing through greatest elongations the inferior planets can appear stationary due to the geometry of motion and the observer's perspective; Mercury stationary at elongations of ~15–20°, Venus at about ~29° (though Venus's greatest elongation is ~47°).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explanation: when the planet's motion is directly towards or away from the spectator it projects to the same point on the celestial sphere. Earth’s motion shifts the precise stationary points; provide numerical approximate elongations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Phases of inferior planets (Moon-like phases)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mercury and Venus exhibit phases like the Moon: horned (less than half illuminated) near inferior conjunction, gibbous or full-like near superior conjunction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: At superior conjunction whole illuminated disk faces Earth (but usually lost in Sun's glare); illustrated in Fig. 52. Phases explain apparent size vs brightness trade-offs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Greatest brilliancy does not coincide with fullest phase
rubrics_metrics.description: For Venus, maximum apparent brightness occurs a little within greatest elongation, not at full phase, because at full (superior conjunction) the planet is farther and in twilight; near greatest elongation it is nearer and visible at favorable altitude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Venus can be bright enough to cast a shadow and sometimes visible in daylight; brightness depends on both illuminated fraction and distance/altitude relative to twilight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rotational period determination by telescopic surface marks
rubrics_metrics.description: Diurnal rotation of Mercury and Venus is nearly the same as Earth's (~24 hours), determined via tracking spots or marks with the telescope (by analogy to determining solar rotation via sunspots).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides method of measurement: identify and follow a spot/mark across the disk to infer axial rotation period.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transits — definition and why they occur only near nodes
rubrics_metrics.description: A transit is the passage of Mercury or Venus across the Sun's disk (appearing as a small black spot). Transits occur only when an inferior conjunction happens near the point where the planet's orbit crosses the ecliptic (a node).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because orbits are inclined, most inferior conjunctions project the planet above or below the solar disk; only conjunctions at nodes produce transits. Hence transits are restricted to certain months (Mercury in May & November; Venus in June & December). Diagrams explain geometry (Fig. 50).

rubrics_metrics.name: Predictable periodicities of transits (Mercury and Venus patterns)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mercury transits can repeat after intervals of 7, 13, or 33 years depending on orbital resonances; Venus shows an 8-year near-repeat and a long 235-year cycle between returns at the same node.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains resonance ratios (e.g., Mercury ~29 revolutions vs 7 of Earth; Venus 8 Earth years ≈ 13 Venus years) and historical examples (transits in 1761, 1769; predicted 1874). Use these periodicities to anticipate transit opportunities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using transits to determine the sun's horizontal parallax (experimental criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Transits of Venus furnish the most accurate means for determining the sun's horizontal parallax and thus the distance from Earth to Sun; compare Venus's apparent position on the solar disk as seen from widely separated observers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To maximize measurable difference, observers should be stationed at very distant points on Earth; measure precise moments of external/internal contact (timing of contacts is critical); historical coordinated expeditions (e.g., 1761/1769) were mounted for this purpose. The method can yield parallax to within a fraction of a second (text cites ~8.6" for the Sun). Nontrivial trigonometry is required to translate observations to parallax.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transit observations can indicate planetary atmospheres
rubrics_metrics.description: Observations during Venus transits sometimes showed a penumbral light or ligament at immersion/emersion suggesting an atmosphere around Venus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observers noted delayed emersion and a dark 'ligament' that broke like separating drops; such phenomena and twilight effects were interpreted as evidence of an atmosphere of density/extent comparable to Earth's.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tide behaviour depends on depth, channel regularity, and coastal geometry
rubrics_metrics.description: Derivative (propagated) tides depend principally on channel depth and regularity; shallow or irregular parts retard tide-wave causing irregular tides and different directions from primitive tides raised by sun and moon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: tides along shores travel slower than in neighboring sea due to shoals and indented coasts; convex tide-wave lines around islands can blend to create anomalies; Bay of Fundy's high tides ascribed to forcing into a narrow arm. Large lakes/inland seas lack perceptible tides because their size is small relative to the distances to sun/moon; primitive tidal effects require appreciable spatial extent. Apparent anomalies to gravitational theory are often due to local causes and impediments.
